title: Ethics Opinion KBA E-457 — The Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
author: Kentucky Bar Association Ethics Committee

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts selective, human-led AI deployment and materially develops the cluster’s governance account by translating it into concrete professional duties: lawyers must verify outputs, remain accountable for work product, protect confidentiality, supervise users and establish firm-specific policies. It also reinforces adaptive, use-context-specific governance rather than a fixed technical rule.

The Committee does not intend to specify what AI policy an attorney should follow because it is the responsibility of each attorney to best determine how AI will be used within their law firm and then to establish an AI policy that addresses the benefits and risks associated with AI products.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts

st.an: KBA E-457 supports the cluster’s risk-calibrated preference for lawyer-supervised AI: it recognizes efficiency and client-cost benefits while emphasizing professional competence and risks from inaccuracy, bias and opacity. Its support is limited because it does not directly examine unrepresented users’ verification capacity, effective remedies or whether direct-to-consumer deployment shifts risk downward.

st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s central balance: AI may reduce costs and improve efficiency, but those benefits do not displace protection and accountability. st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: KBA E-457 aligns closely with the cluster’s principal proposition: existing professional duties govern lawyers’ AI use, but responsible compliance requires active understanding of the technology and scrutiny of provider information-handling practices. Its interim status and openness to future rule amendments also fit the cluster’s view that the need for AI-specific regulation remains unsettled.
qs: Whether the attorney is researching relevant case law, reviewing documents, or drafting court pleadings, care must be taken that the attorney understands how AI works, how it may be used responsibly and in conjunction with the Supreme Court Rules of Professional Conduct.

The Ethics Committee has issued Ethics Opinions discussing the ever-changing environment of technology and its application to the Rules, and many of these Opinions are applicable to AI.7 In addition to the guidance provided by these Opinions, we caution lawyers that before using an AI product they review the provider’s privacy policies and its disclaimers in handling client and attorney information.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: KBA E-457 aligns closely with the cluster’s supervised-AI model. It keeps lawyers accountable for AI-assisted work, requires verification of legal research, applies existing ethical duties to tool use, and adds confidentiality, fee, training and policy safeguards. It recognizes potential efficiency gains but does not directly assess whether verification consumes those gains.

kp.k: Existing professional duties govern AI use
kp.d: The Committee applies Kentucky's existing professional conduct rules to AI rather than announcing AI-specific rules. Its March 15, 2024 opinion offers interim guidance while the Kentucky Bar Association's AI Task Force considers responsible use and possible rule amendments. It acknowledges unresolved questions and excludes advertising rules from its scope; the formally adopted opinion is advisory only.
qs: In the interim it is intended that this Opinion will provide some practical guidance while the Task Force explores multiple AI issues and whether amendments to the Rules of Professional Conduct are appropriate to address the unique applications a lawyer faces in the use of AI.
This Rule provides that formal opinions are advisory only.

kp.d: The Committee interprets Kentucky's competence obligation as requiring lawyers to understand AI's uses, benefits and risks and continuously update their knowledge. It goes further conditionally: as tools improve and become widespread, failure to use an available AI tool may breach competence duties. This is a prospective warning, not an unconditional requirement to adopt every tool.
qs: In essence, the rapid development of AI poses challenges for attorneys to continuously update their knowledge base in order to maintain their competence.
lawyers need to be aware that not using an available AI tool may constitute a failure to meet the lawyer’s duty of attaining and maintaining competence under Rule 1.1.

kp.k: AI offers potential task efficiencies, not demonstrated outcomes
kp.d: The opinion lists suggested benefits spanning research, document review and summarisation, repetitive-task automation, deception detection, outcome prediction, client responses and continuous information access. It anticipates faster, cheaper services but supplies no measured productivity results. Its expectation that AI may become commonplace is explicitly prospective.
qs: Streamlining legal research to find relevant case law, statutes, and precedents more quickly;
Reducing legal expenses to the client due to accelerated research and document preparation.
In the near future, using AI may become as commonplace as an attorney’s current use of other technological systems which have now become an indispensable part of the practice of law.

kp.k: Accuracy, bias and opacity constrain AI benefits
kp.d: The Committee identifies risks including misunderstanding complex legal concepts, biased decision-making, opaque reasoning, confidential information disclosure and fabricated authorities. It also warns that duplicative or irrelevant AI output may increase discovery production expenses, qualifying the expectation of cost savings. These are qualitative risk statements rather than measured error rates.
qs: AI may struggle to grasp complex legal concepts which can produce inaccuracies and misinterpretations;
AI models trained on biased data may perpetuate biases in the legal decision-making process;
AI may provide duplicative and/or irrelevant materials which may increase discovery production expenses.

kp.k: Routine research disclosure has important exceptions
kp.d: Routine AI-generated research does not itself require specific client disclosure. The opinion identifies exceptions where the client pays research costs, a third-party service provides the research, or court or other rules require disclosure. Outsourcing should be communicated, and an outside AI service's receipt of protected client information requires client consent.
qs: Thus, routine use of AI generated research in a client’s matter does not in and of itself require specific communication to the client, unless the client is being charged for the cost of the research,
If an outside AI service will be receiving information protected by the lawyer’s duty of confidentiality under SCR 3.130(1.6), then obtaining client consent is required.

kp.k: AI efficiencies must inform reasonable fees
kp.d: Under Kentucky's fee-reasonableness rules, the Committee says reduced work through successful AI use must be reflected in charges, with fee reductions considered where appropriate. Hourly lawyers cannot bill time not actually spent, and savings should reach clients. The opinion uses In re Burghoff, involving copied internet material rather than generative AI, as an illustration: 17 of 19 brief pages were copied, and charging 25.5 hours was found unreasonable given the actual labour.
qs: Accordingly, the attorney’s charge for legal services must be adjusted to recognize the reduced legal work devoted to a client’s matter when there is a successful result by virtue of using AI.
It should be obvious that lawyers may not charge a client for hours not actually spent on a client’s matter.

Further, the Court found that the attorney violated the ethics Rules by charging his client for 25.5 hours of legal work in preparing the briefs which was unreasonable given the actual labor invested in copying the article from the internet.

kp.k: Client AI expenses require advance written agreement
kp.d: The opinion permits reimbursement for AI usage expenses with advance agreement confirmed in writing, explaining anticipated costs, their basis and payment terms. It notes an existing-client billing exception where the established basis continues, with changes communicated. Learning AI, keeping current and maintaining AI services are treated as overhead rather than client-chargeable training costs.
qs: If the client is to bear these expenses, then before the charge can be made, the client’s written consent must first be obtained.

If the lawyer intends to charge the client for AI expenses and the client agrees to pay these expenses, then the lawyer should explain, in writing and in advance, the anticipated cost of those expenses, the basis for the cost being billed, and the terms of payment.
However, similar to the lawyer’s cost of general overhead expenses, the costs of AI training and keeping abreast of AI developments should not be charged to clients.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires provider diligence and secure inputs
kp.d: Lawyers retain responsibility for client confidentiality when using AI, including understanding provider retention, training and third-party sharing practices. The Committee recommends reviewing terms and disclaimers and avoiding inadequately protected client inputs unless consent is obtained. It warns that hypothetical questions may still expose identities or matters through sophisticated inference.
qs: Some generative AI products utilize inputted information or uploaded documents such as pleadings or contracts to train itself, or to share that information with third parties.
Hence, an attorney should take care that any information inputted into a generative AI product does not identify the client or the nature of the representation.
the use of hypotheticals is only permissible as long as there is no reasonable likelihood that anyone will be able to determine who the client is or what the client matter involves.

kp.k: Provider assurances leave privilege and disclosure questions unresolved
kp.d: The Committee says written assurances against off-site transmission or third-party sharing may permit confidential inputs, but warns that confidentiality may remain difficult to establish. At the opinion's date, it describes discoverability and privilege-waiver consequences of AI sharing as judicially unresolved. Where inadvertent disclosure remains a concern, it recommends informed consent covering uses, risks, benefits and privacy concerns, while noting that Kentucky then had no similar pending rules requiring blanket advance permission.
qs: If that promise is confirmed in writing, then it may be allowable to input the client’s confidential information with that provider.
it has not yet been judicially determined whether sharing information with an AI program would render that information discoverable, and/or result in waiving claims of attorney-client privilege.
The attorney should discuss with the client the proposed use of AI, the applications of AI to be utilized, the risks and benefits of the AI product, and fully explain

kp.k: Human verification and candor remain mandatory
kp.d: Lawyers must check AI-assisted pleadings for factual and citation accuracy, monitor jurisdiction-specific AI disclosure and certification requirements, and correct discovered inaccuracies. The opinion cites Mata v. Avianca as a sanctions incident involving fake AI-generated cases and subsequent failure to be candid, not as evidence of a model error rate. Verification remains the lawyer's responsibility regardless of a tool's apparent credibility.
qs: Attorneys who use AI provider services like ChatGPT have a responsibility to check their pleadings for accuracy in their references to both facts and legal citations.

Two New York lawyers were recently sanctioned after the Court found they filed a brief that contained numerous fake, GAI case law citations, when they later failed to “come clean” with the Court about their use.
If an attorney later discovers an inaccuracy, then the attorney is required to correct the inaccuracy, and to notify the Court of any misleading statements.

kp.k: Partners must institutionalise AI supervision and training
kp.d: Partners, managers and supervising lawyers must establish measures supporting compliance by lawyers and supervised nonlawyers, employees and contractors. The Committee recommends firm-specific AI policies, updated cybersecurity practices and training rather than a fixed policy template likely to become obsolete. Adopting Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1's reasoning, it treats AI work product as requiring human review comparable to nonlawyer assistance, with ultimate responsibility remaining with lawyers.
qs: Lawyers are ultimately responsible for the work product that they create regardless of whether that work product was originally drafted or researched by a nonlawyer or generative AI.
Functionally, this means a lawyer must verify the accuracy and sufficiency of all research performed by generative AI.
Creating a culture of security and privacy of client information may be best attained through training everyone on the law firm’s AI policies and focusing on human error and behavior.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Kentucky Bar Association Ethics Committee presents AI as potentially transformative for legal-service efficiency, while requiring continuing lawyer responsibility and safeguards.
pts.d: The Committee identifies suggested benefits including faster research, large-volume document analysis, repetitive-task automation, deception detection, outcome prediction, faster client responses, continuous access to information and reduced client expenses. These are presented as potential benefits, not measured findings. It predicts that AI could become commonplace and that, as tools improve and adoption spreads, failure to use an available tool could constitute a competence failure. It also identifies inaccurate or fabricated output, bias, opacity, confidentiality exposure, cybersecurity threats and potentially increased discovery expenses. Its ethical guidance retains human responsibility: lawyers must verify AI work, comply with court requirements, correct inaccuracies and supervise staff through policies and training. AI-generated efficiencies should benefit clients rather than support inflated hourly bills; appropriate fee reductions and advance written agreement for AI expenses are required. Routine AI research does not itself require disclosure, subject to outsourcing, client charges and court-rule exceptions. These are the Committee’s interpretations of ethical duties, rather than predictions of workforce displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies principally on professional-conduct rules, prior ethics opinions, illustrative cases and commentary, rather than empirical measurements of AI productivity or accuracy.
pts.d: The Committee grounds competence, communication, billing, confidentiality, candor and supervision duties in Kentucky’s SCR 3.130 and its comments. It draws analogies from previous guidance on cloud computing, cybersecurity and outsourcing, and quotes Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1 on lawyer verification of AI research. Mata v. Avianca illustrates fabricated citations and sanctions, not a measured hallucination rate. In re Burghoff illustrates unreasonable billing and plagiarism involving internet material, not an AI deployment. Efficiency and widespread-adoption claims have no quantified supporting study in the opinion. Confidentiality and cybersecurity discussion draws on an executive order and published expert commentary; the quoted human-involvement figure for data breaches is general cybersecurity commentary, not an AI-specific measurement. The opinion is formally adopted but advisory.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 15, 2024 opinion offers interim guidance, distinguishes current duties from conditional future adoption, and stresses unresolved risks.
pts.d: The opinion describes existing AI use in spell-checking and legal-research functions, with wider integration anticipated in the unspecified near future. The possibility that non-use could breach competence is conditional on tools becoming more refined and widespread, not an unconditional present mandate to use generative AI. Billing adjustments depend on actual work saved and reasonableness; charging AI expenses requires advance client agreement confirmed in writing, while training and keeping abreast of developments are overhead. Disclosure exceptions concern charged research, third-party services and applicable court rules; the opinion requires consent where an outside service receives protected information. Written provider assurances may permit confidential inputs, but the Committee treats confidentiality verification and privilege consequences as unresolved. Its guidance is interim pending task-force work and further experience, with current rules to be checked before reliance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Kentucky lawyers, supervising partners and managers, law-firm personnel, clients and courts.
pts.d: Practising lawyers face continuing technological education, verification, confidentiality and court-compliance responsibilities while potentially delivering faster and cheaper services. Partners, managers and supervising lawyers must implement appropriate policies and training for lawyers, nonlawyer personnel and supervised contractors. Clients may receive cost savings and quicker responses, but face inaccurate work, privacy exposure and possible sanctions; prospective and former clients also fall within the opinion’s confidentiality discussion. Courts are affected by fabricated authorities and responses through verification or certification requirements. The opinion does not distinguish effects by firm size or market tier and does not predict lawyer job losses, staffing restructuring or competitive market shares. Around-the-clock legal information is listed as a potential benefit, without an evidenced claim that AI closes the justice gap.
